Thurgood Marshall. A pioneering civil rights lawyer who became the first African-American Supreme Court Justice, using the law as a weapon against segregation and discrimination. As chief counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, he argued Brown v. Board of Education and a string of landmark cases that dismantled the legal architecture of Jim Crow, fundamentally transforming American society. He led the legal challenge to segregation, developing a strategy to chip away at the separate but equal doctrine. In 1954 he argued Brown v. Board of Education before the Supreme Court, successfully challenging school segregation as inherently unequal and unconstitutional. By 1967 he had argued thirty-two cases before the Supreme Court, winning twenty-nine of them—an extraordinary trial record that established him as a constitutional master. In 1961 President Kennedy appointed him to the U.S. Court of Appeals, and in 1967 President Lyndon Johnson appointed him to the Supreme Court. He served twenty-four years as a Supreme Court Justice from 1967 to 1991, writing opinions that expanded civil rights, criminal procedure protections, and voting rights. Throughout his civil rights career, he faced fierce Southern opposition and death threats, yet remained committed to nonviolent legal struggle. He was the complementary strategist to Martin Luther King Jr.—Marshall fought in courts while King mobilized in the streets. Rosa Parks's arrest became part of cases Marshall's organization supported and strategized around. Younger activists like John Lewis benefited from the legal victories Marshall secured. And Brown v. Board of Education was his signature case, the pivotal Supreme Court decision that changed everything.
